items.title: Bombay High Court quashes Customs order flagged for citing non-existent AI-generated judgments
items.summary: The Bombay High Court recently set aside a customs department order after taking note of concerns that the adjudicating authority had relied on non-existent, artificial intelligence (AI) generated Supreme Court judgments [ Quanta Logistics Pvt Ltd v. Commissioner of Customs (Import-I) ]. A Bench of Justices MS Karnik and Sandesh D Patil quashed an August 11, 2026 order passed by the customs commissioner against Quanta Logistics. Justice MS Karnik, Justice Sandesh Patil Quanta argued that the customs authority passed the order by resorting to AI without an independent application of mind. Senior Advocate Venkatesh Dhond demonstrated that the order cited two Supreme Court judgments that did not exist in any database, describing them as possible AI hallucinations. When Quanta requested for copies of the cited judgment, the department failed to provide the same. Senior Advocate Venkatesh Dhond The petitioner relied on the 2026 Supreme Court decision in Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya v. Union of India, in which the apex court had emphasised on a "zero-tolerance" approach to tackling the use of AI-generated precedents without due verification. In response, the Customs department agreed that the order under challenge could be quashed and the matter reconsidered. Consequently, the High Court quashed the Customs order by consent and directed the petitioner to appear before the authority so that the matter can be examined afresh. Dhond appeared along with advocates Bimal Rajasekhar and Sunand Subramaniam for Quanta. Advocates Jitendra B Mishra and Sangeeta Yadav appeared for the Customs department. [Read order]

items.title: Outraging modesty provision under BNS applies to transgender women: Bombay High Court
items.summary: The Nagpur Bench of the Bombay High Court has ruled that a transgender person who identifies as a woman can also invoke legal provisions meant to protect a woman's modesty under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) [Vishal Sunil Ingle v. State of Maharashtra]. Justice Mehroz K Pathan on November 3, 2026 dismissed a criminal revision application filed by the accused, Vishal Sunil Ingle. He had challenged the rejection of his discharge application. “The perusal of the FIR would show that the complainant/victim has identified herself to be a woman and the aforesaid self determination cannot be questioned at least at the present stage while accused is seeking discharge,” the judge said. Justice Mehroz K Pathan He concluded that “allegations of assault and outraging the modesty of a woman can be sustained even where the victim is a transgender person who identifies herself as a woman.” The accused, an Agniveer in the Indian Army, faced charges under Section 75 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Section 18(D) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019. The complainant alleged that the applicant committed sexual assault under a false promise of marriage in October 2025. The defense counsel argued that Section 75 of the BNS strictly applies to a ‘woman’ defined as a female human being and, therefore, cannot apply to a transgender victim. The defense also highlighted that the victim received a formal transgender identity certificate only after the alleged incidents took place. The Bench dismissed these arguments and emphasised on the legal right to self-perceived gender identity. items.title: NMC founder BR Shetty held liable for $5.4 billion healthcare fraud by Abu Dhabi court
items.summary: The Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) Court has held NMC Healthcare founder BR Shetty and former Chief Executive Officer Prasanth Manghat liable for fraudulent and wrongful trading in connection with a massive financial fraud that led to the collapse of the healthcare group in 2020. Justice Sir Andrew Smith of the ADGM Court of First Instance held that both Shetty and Manghat had knowingly participated in a fraudulent scheme involving the misappropriation of company funds, concealment of borrowings and manipulation of financial statements. The Court identified $5.397 billion as the starting point for assessing the financial contributions that the two would be required to make towards the company's assets. The November 5 judgment revealed that over 500 transfers were made into Shetty's personal bank accounts. These transfers totalled AED 4.18 billion, with net payments of approximately AED 2.6 billion after accounting for funds returned to the group. The case arose from the collapse of NMC Health, which Shetty founded in Abu Dhabi in 1975. The company was listed on the London Stock Exchange in 2012 and subsequently became part of the FTSE 100 index. According to the administrators, NMC's management diverted substantial company funds for personal use while concealing billions of dollars in borrowings. The Court examined more than 500 transfers into Shetty's personal bank accounts, involving AED 4.18 billion. After accounting for funds transferred back to the group, the net payments amounted to approximately AED 2.6 billion. The transactions also involved expenditure on private aircraft, properties in Dubai Hills and investments in a Wyoming oil field. The fraud extended to NMC's financial statements. By December 2018, the group had accumulated approximately $3.88 billion in undisclosed borrowings while reporting debts of only $1.99 billion. The Court found that the group used sham supplier transactions to disguise borrowings. Under these arrangements, suppliers raised invoices for goods or services that were not intended to be supplied. Banks financed the invoices and the funds were channelled back into the group. The Court rejected Shetty's defence that he was himself a victim of fraud perpetrated by senior executives. It also rejected Manghat's argument that he lacked control over the company's financial affairs. items.title: ED is not super cop: Karnataka High Court quashes money laundering probe against Congress leader
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently quashed an Enforcement Directorate (ED) money laundering investigation naming Congress leader KY Nanje Gowda, stating that the agency was not a 'super cop' to investigate every case. [YB Ashwathanarayan v. Union of India] . Karnataka High Court ED is not a super cop to investigate anything and everything which comes into its notice. Justice MI Arun said that the ED could only prosecute as long as a foundational criminal offence is pending. "The power of the ED is derivative and not original. It cannot initiate an investigation suo motu based on a standalone suspicion of money laundering. If there is no existence of the predicate offence, then in that event, proceedings under PMLA cannot exist; meaning even when the predicate offence is terminated in favour of the accused therein, the proceedings under PMLA cannot continue." The Court further emphasised on the separation of powers between organs of government to outline the authority of the ED under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). "Law recognizes the requirements of checks and balances. The ED is not a super cop to investigate anything and everything which comes into its notice. Section 48 of the PMLA envisages the authorities under the Act. Once appointed under the PMLA, they are bound by the restraints imposed on them by the PMLA. Section 66(2) of PMLA envisages that if the ED is of the opinion that it is having certain materials which constitute a scheduled offence, then in that event, the same should be forwarded to the concerned agency. The Act does not expressly empower the ED or the authorities under the PMLA to prefer a private complaint in respect of a scheduled offence and on the strength of it, thereafter, take up investigation against the accused therein under the provisions of PMLA." items.title: Bengaluru ADR Week 2026 to be held from November 13 to 15
items.summary: The third edition of Bengaluru ADR Week will be held from November 13 to 15, 2026, with judges, senior advocates and arbitration practitioners from India and abroad expected to participate in the three-day conference. The conference, organised by the Bengaluru ADR Week Organising Committee, will focus on the theme "ADR: Diverse Perspectives. Viable Resolutions. One Sustainable Ecosystem." Former Supreme Court judges Justices RV Raveendran, L Nageswara Rao, S Ravindra Bhat and Abhay S Oka will be among the prominent participants. Karnataka High Court Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and several sitting judges of the High Court, including Justices DK Singh, BM Shyam Prasad, Sunil Dutt Yadav, SR Krishna Kumar, Sachin Shankar Magadum, R Nataraj, ER Indiresh, MGS Kamal, Tara Vitasta Ganju and CM Poonacha , are also expected to participate. The conference will feature discussions on the growing role of artificial intelligence in arbitration, the expanding scope of alternative dispute resolution (ADR), institutional independence, arbitral appointments and ethical standards. A session titled "A Made for India ADR Model: What should we change?" will examine the need for changes to India's existing dispute resolution framework. Other discussions will focus on challenges in enforcing arbitral awards and whether confidentiality surrounding such awards is holding back the development of arbitration. A special roundtable on "Making Bengaluru a seat of choice: A roadmap for Karnataka" will explore measures to position the city as a preferred destination for domestic and international arbitration. The conference will also feature a debate on whether domestic arbitral awards should be subject to a statutory first appeal. Karnataka Advocate General K Shashi Kiran Shetty and Senior Advocates Aditya Sondhi, Gaurav Pachnanda and Jayna Kothari are among the speakers. International participants will include representatives from White & Case, Linklaters, Baker Botts and the Singapore International Arbitration Centre. Representatives from leading Indian law firms and in-house legal teams will also participate. The event has received support from the Karnataka High Court, the Arbitration and Conciliation Centre, Bengaluru (Domestic and International), and the Advocates Association of Bangalore. items.title: Animal, Pushpa, KGF: When cinema turns violence into heroism | Let Me Explain 176 | Pooja Prasanna
items.summary: A 15-year-old girl was attacked with a chainsaw inside her classroom in Andhra Pradesh. The brutality of the attack shocked people across the country. After the initial shock, another conversation started. Many began pointing to films such as Animal, KGF and Pushpa, where extreme violence is presented as an expression of masculinity, anger and power. And then came a response from the overlord of alpha-male cinema, director Sandeep Reddy Vanga. He said that when a horrific crime takes place, the first response should be empathy for the victim. He accused critics of using the incident as an opportunity to target filmmakers and said cinema was being made a scapegoat. Watching a movie with violence alone does not automatically make someone violent. There is little evidence to establish such a direct cause-and-effect relationship. But that is also a rather simplistic way of looking at the criticism.Because the question is not just whether films make people violent. It is about what kind of violence we are normalising, what kind of masculinity we are celebrating, and what happens when brutality is repeatedly presented as an expression of love, anger and heroism. items.title: Prakash Raj meets Kalady Uni students, says he will join their hunger strike if needed
items.summary: In solidarity with the protesting students of Keralam’s Kalady Sree Sankaracharya University of Sanskrit, actor Praksh Raj said that he would join their hunger strike if they are not allowed to write exams. The actor met with the 16 suspended students on Saturday, November 7, and said that the state government and the higher education minister, Roji M John, must take accountability for the future of the students. "I have come here for a protest, but I promise that if this continues, I will come and sit with them here. I have no problem. I can stop everything and come and sit here," Prakash Raj said. The actor questioned how long the university would continue suppressing dissent among young students. "What is this anarchy, dictatorial behaviour of the university or the education minister of this state? How long will everybody become like Modi and the Central government to stop youngsters from protesting and asking questions?" he asked. "This generation is not Savarkar's to write sorry petitions. This generation protests with the strength of what Gandhi has taught them and asks questions with the rights Babasaheb Ambedkar has given them. This is not Manusmriti, this is the Constitution," he said. The actor also thanked the SFI and DYFI, as well as other youth organisations for supporting the protesting students. The students have been on a hunger strike for the past six days. The dispute arose from a protest held on the university campus on August 13, 2026, during a Syndicate meeting. The university accused the students of staging a mock funeral of Vice-Chancellor Ciza Thomas, manhandling her and attempting to damage her vehicle as she left the campus. The students, however, maintained that the demonstration was part of a street play organised to highlight the longstanding neglect of the university's Theatre Department. Two FIRs were registered at the Kalady police station in connection with the incident. The university subsequently suspended the students on September 1, pending disciplinary proceedings. On November 3, the Kerala High Court allowed an appeal filed by the university, headed by Vice-Chancellor Ciza Thomas, against the Single Bench order permitting 16 students to appear for examinations scheduled to begin on November 4. The Court held that they had not established their eligibility under the university regulations, including the minimum attendance requirement.
